title: Equine in its length
html_source:
“Equine” means horse-like– we might today say “horse-faced”.

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: We might well, but we probably wouldn’t say “his face was horse-faced in its length”.

The adjective doesn’t necessarily suggest a close resemblance to a horse’s face, only a proportionate lengthiness. Can people have long faces that are non-horsey? Is lengthiness essential to horsiness, or just highly correlative?

I suppose here “equine” is also a subtle dig at Mulligan, much the same way as the word “stately” gives him an air of uppitiness or grandness that is both genuine and affected.
